USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold current posture and allow the Section 301 investigation to conclude before taking further tariff action. The US has significant leverage — strong economy, bipartisan political support, and documented evidence of Chinese IP theft — but premature escalation before the investigation produces its findings would sacrifice legal and diplomatic positioning. Use this window to build the evidentiary record and coordinate with allies.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: As of March 2018, the US faces a low-to-moderate threat from the trade dispute, but holds a position of relative strength. The Section 301 investigation initiated August 2017 has produced substantial evidence of Chinese forced technology transfer, cyber-enabled IP theft, and discriminatory licensing practices (USTR investigation, Federal Register notice Aug 24 2017). Trump's November 2018 Beijing visit yielded commercial MOUs but no structural IP concessions, confirming that diplomatic engagement alone will not resolve the issue. The Section 201 tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (Jan 22 2018) represent a modest first action, and the Commerce Department has recommended aggressive Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs (Feb 16 2018), with Trump's decision deadline of April 11 for steel.

The US economy is strong: industrial production rising steadily (101.7, up 0.7%), consumer sentiment robust (99.7), CPI moderate (249.5), and the Fed gradually tightening (1.42%). The dollar has weakened slightly from its Oct 2017 peak (108.4 vs 112.1), which actually helps US export competitiveness. Oil prices at $61/barrel are up 26% but manageable. Corporate bond yields (4.55%) are elevated but spreads are healthy. This macro backdrop gives the US room to act without urgency.

However, China has signaled it will 'take all necessary measures' against unilateral US action (Commerce Ministry spokesman Gao Feng). Retaliation could target US agricultural exports, aerospace, or US companies operating in China. The 301 investigation is the strongest card — it provides a legal foundation, political cover, and international legitimacy that premature broad tariffs would not. Conservative leaders have called it 'a good first step' (IPWatchdog, Jan 24 2018). The investigation's one-year deadline runs to August 2018, but reports suggest affirmative findings could come earlier (Orrick analysis, Jan 20 2018). Waiting for the investigation to conclude gives the US a stronger hand: documented findings, coordinated allied support (Japan/EU share concerns about forced tech transfer), and a clear legal basis for targeted remedies. Premature broad tariffs risk alienating allies, triggering market volatility, and giving China a propaganda win as defender of free trade.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation ongoing with strong evidence of Chinese IP theft and forced technology transfer
US economy strong: industrial production rising, consumer sentiment 99.7, moderate inflation
Commerce Dept recommended Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs (Feb 16 2018) — Trump decision pending by April
China warned of 'all necessary measures' against unilateral US action
Bipartisan domestic support for tough stance on China
Weakened dollar (108.4 vs 112.1 peak) improves US export competitiveness
Allies (Japan, EU) share US concerns about Chinese forced technology transfer

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit)
Dollar Index: 108.4 (Feb 28 2018), down from 112.1 Oct 2017 peak
Sources close to the investigation have disclosed that the USTR will announce an affirmative finding and make remedy recommendations sometime this month
Commerce Department recommends 24% global tariff on steel or 53% on 12 countries including China; Trump must respond by April 11 and 19
